title: PART I

nodes.title: Boeing Business and Reportable Segments
nodes.summary: Boeing describes itself as a major aerospace company organized into four segments. Commercial Airplanes develops and sells jetliners, including the 737, 767, 777 and 787, while ending 747 production in 2022 and continuing 777X and 737-7/-10 development. Defense, Space & Security develops and modifies military aircraft, weapons, defense and intelligence systems, satellites and space-exploration products. Global Services supports commercial and defense customers with logistics, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, parts, training, documentation and digital services. Boeing Capital finances customer purchases and manages exposure through leases, receivables, assets and investments.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The company owns numerous patents and licenses others’ patents related to its products and manufacturing, while also licensing intellectual property to and from third parties. The U.S. government may use or authorize use of inventions developed under government contracts. Unpatented research, development and engineering capabilities, trademarks, trade secrets, and other IP also support the business. Although IP is important across its operations, the company does not expect any single right’s expiration or patent-license termination to materially affect the business.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.summary: Boeing reports workforce size and international representation for 2021–22, union membership and major agreements, and its commitments to diversity, equity and inclusion, including workforce demographics and employee resource groups. It describes competitive benefits, hiring and retention, employee feedback and recognition, and professional development through learning and tuition programs. It also emphasizes workplace safety, quality, integrity and sustainability, annual Code of Conduct commitments, channels for raising concerns, and responses to employee issues.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The commercial jet market and airline industry face intense competition, including Airbus and Chinese entrants; the company aims to compete through better products and processes, lower costs, and superior aircraft and services. Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS) competes with major U.S. contractors, SpaceX, and expanding non-U.S. firms, sometimes in competitor teams, and expects strong competition through 2023. Boeing Global Services (BGS) faces similarly tough competition and plans to grow share by using its lifecycle services network, customer satisfaction, and productivity.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
key_items: Government Contracts; Commercial Aircraft; Non-U.S. Sales
nodes.summary: The company operates in heavily regulated U.S. and international markets. Government contracts may be terminated for convenience or default, with different payment, reprocurement-cost, and damages consequences. Commercial aircraft must meet aviation production, safety, repair, airworthiness, installation, and certification requirements. Environmental laws govern hazardous materials and may address climate change, creating compliance, energy, materials, and technology costs; remediation is routine, but stricter rules or newly discovered contamination could materially affect results, finances, or cash flows. Environmental contingencies are discussed in a financial-statement note. Non-U.S. sales face trade, investment, currency, anti-corruption, earnings-repatriation, political, and economic risks.

nodes.title: Raw Materials, Parts and Subassemblies
nodes.summary: Boeing relies on suppliers for key aerospace materials, components and subassemblies; alternative material sources may take a year or more to qualify. It stopped buying Russian titanium in 2022 without operational disruption, using inventory and alternative sources, and manages sole-source supply relationships. Supplier failures, cost or energy constraints could harm schedules, profitability and customer commitments despite oversight systems. The text notes the business is not materially seasonal, directs readers to Part III for executive officers, provides corporate history, headquarters and contact details, and explains website and SEC filing access. It also describes forward-looking statements, where they appear, identifying terms and examples.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
nodes.summary:
Item 1A. Risk Factors
An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties and our actual results and future trends may differ materially from our past or projected future performance. We urge investors to consider carefully the risk factors described below in evaluating the information contained in this report.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Operations
We depend heavily on commercial airlines, subjecting us to unique risks.
key_items: Market conditions have a significant impact on demand for our commercial aircraft and related services

We enter into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns or if increases in our costs exceed the applicable escalation rate
We derive a significant portion of our revenues from a limited number of commercial airlines
nodes.summary: The company’s reliance on commercial airlines exposes it to risks from cyclical, competitive markets and factors affecting traffic and aircraft demand, including economic and political conditions, airline profitability and financing, trade and government relations, technology, competition, fuel prices, security threats, health crises, and environmental rules. Deterioration in the economy, industry, or major customers may reduce, delay, or cancel orders and payments, harming revenue, profits, cash flow, backlog, and deliveries over several years. Fixed-price contracts with indexed escalation create losses if costs exceed escalation; fluctuating indices can materially affect revenue and margins. Revenue is concentrated among a limited number of airlines, whose options, commitments, purchases, fleet choices, consolidations, or financial difficulties may reduce sales and profits. Airlines also face rising fuel and other costs amid high inflation.

nodes.title: Our Commercial Airplanes business depends on our ability to maintain a healthy production system, ensure every airplane in our production system conforms to our exacting specifications, achieve planned production rate targets, successfully develop and certify new aircraft or new derivative aircraft, and meet or exceed stringent performance and reliability standards.
key_items: We must minimize disruption caused by production changes, achieve operational stability and implement productivity improvements in order to meet customer demand and maintain our profitabillty
If our commercial aircraft fail to satisfy performance and reliability requirements and/or potentially required sustainability standards, we could face additional costs and/or lower revenues
nodes.summary: Boeing’s commercial-aircraft performance depends on safe, reliable production, meeting schedules and targets, and developing and certifying new aircraft amid complex supplier, workforce, and regulatory demands. The text explains evolving FAA rules for 737 MAX safety enhancements, related retrofit costs and certification risks, and possible stricter foreign regulations. Quality problems and supply-chain issues have delayed deliveries, exposing Boeing to customer compensation, order termination, or substitutions. Production-rate changes and plans for the 787, 777X, and 737 carry disruption and cost risks; COVID-related constraints, labor instability, and inflation have hurt productivity and financial results. Operational, supplier, certification, performance, reliability, and potential sustainability failures could further delay deliveries, raise costs, reduce revenue and margins, and increase warranty or support expenses.

nodes.title: Changes in levels of U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities could negatively impact our financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The company’s substantial U.S. government and defense revenue is exposed to unpredictable spending, delayed or temporary appropriations, shutdowns, budget pressure, and changing DoD, NASA, and other agency priorities, potentially reducing, delaying, or canceling programs and contracts. Procurement shifts emphasize affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and technical-data/software delivery, requiring adaptation by the company and suppliers. Operations also depend on financially stable subcontractors, skilled labor, and available materials; inflation, pandemic-related disruption, supply constraints, geopolitical events, single-source suppliers, and costly or unavailable inputs could delay delivery and raise costs. Finally, intense domestic and international competition, industry consolidation, customer cost pressure, and U.S. procurement rules may reduce contracts, revenue, and market share across BCA, BDS, and BGS.

nodes.title: Supply Chain, Acquisition Priorities, and Competition Risks
key_items: Our ability to deliver products and services that satisfy customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of highly skilled labor, raw materials and other components.
Competition within our markets and with respect to the products we sell may reduce our future contracts and sales.
nodes.summary: Changing U.S. defense priorities, including affordability, cybersecurity, and technical-data requirements, may affect revenue and market share if the company and suppliers cannot adapt. Delivery depends on supplier stability, skilled labor, and available materials; inflation, COVID-related disruption, labor instability, geopolitical events, single-source reliance, and shortages or high prices could delay production, raise costs, or harm financial results. Intense domestic and international competition, industry consolidation, customer budget pressures, and procurement rules may reduce contracts, sales, revenue, and market share.

nodes.title: We derive a significant portion of our revenues from non-U.S. sales and are subject to the risks of doing business in other countries.
nodes.summary: Approximately 41% of Boeing’s 2022 revenue came from non-U.S. customers, including foreign military sales, and international sales are expected to remain significant. Risks include changing regulations and trade policies, tariffs and restrictions, currency shifts, political and economic instability, local sourcing and industrial participation requirements, customer financing and funding uncertainty, reliance on foreign representatives, complex global operations, legal compliance, taxes, and conflict or other crises. U.S.-China tariffs affect some aircraft components; Boeing uses duty drawback procedures to mitigate costs. China remains an important market, but 737 MAX delivery resumption awaits regulatory approval, and fewer future orders could reduce market share. Russia-related sanctions and export controls led Boeing to suspend operations there, while the Ukraine war has harmed and may further harm results. Further trade deterioration could materially affect Boeing’s financial position, results, or cash flows.

nodes.title: We use estimates and make assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs. Changes in our estimates and/or assumptions could adversely affect our future financial results.
nodes.summary: The text explains that contract and program accounting relies on estimates and assumptions about risks, revenues, costs, schedules, wages, materials, incentives, penalties, claims, and award fees; revisions may harm future results. For commercial aircraft, program accounting allocates production, tooling, nonrecurring, and warranty costs across estimated program units and requires estimates of production quantity and period, prices, and costs. These estimates can change with orders and market outlook, mix, rates, learning curves, escalation, derivatives, supplier or customer issues, and certification risks on development programs. Different assumptions or changed circumstances could materially alter reported revenue and profit; further policy details are cited in the 10-K.

nodes.title: We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures.
nodes.summary: The company may pursue mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, strategic alliances, and divestitures, but cannot assure these will deliver expected benefits. Results depend on integration, portfolio performance, and acquired teams, and may be harmed by performance problems, legacy liabilities, transaction costs, intangible amortization, asset impairments, guarantees, partner performance, indemnifications, or joint-venture consolidation. Divestitures may leave ongoing financial obligations, with nonperformance potentially causing payments, higher costs, or write-downs despite risk-mitigation procedures.

The section covers risks from reliance on cyclical commercial-airline markets and concentrated customers; production quality, supply chains, schedules, certification, new aircraft development, and performance standards; changing U.S. defense spending, acquisition priorities, competition, and supplier availability; and international sales, regulation, trade, currency, political instability, and conflict. It also describes uncertainty in contract and program accounting estimates and the possibility that mergers, acquisitions, alliances, or divestitures fail to deliver expected benefits or create costs and liabilities.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Contracts
key_items: We conduct a significant portion of our business pursuant to U.S. government contracts, which are subject to unique risks.
The U.S. government may modify, curtail or terminate one or more of our contracts
We are subject to U.S. government inquiries and investigations, including periodic audits of costs that we determine are reimbursable under U.S. government contracts
We enter into fixed-price contracts which could subject us to losses if we have cost overruns.
We enter into cost-type contracts, which also carry risks.
We enter into contracts that include in-orbit incentive payments that subject us to risks.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from substantial U.S. government contracting, including regulatory and disclosure costs, withheld payments, contract changes or cancellations, funding uncertainty, audits, repayment demands, penalties, suspension, debarment, and reputational harm. It describes fixed-price contract exposure to overruns, losses, delays, and performance incentives, including examples of affected development programs; cost-type contract risks of reduced fees or cancellation; and satellite in-orbit incentive payments that may be forfeited or refunded if performance standards are not met, potentially causing significant charges.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Cybersecurity and Business Disruptions
key_items: Unauthorized access to our, our customers’ and/or our suppliers’ information and systems could negatively impact our business.
Business disruptions could seriously affect our future sales and financial condition or increase our costs and expenses.
nodes.summary: The text outlines cybersecurity and business-disruption risks. Cyberattacks on Boeing or its supply chain could expose sensitive data or intellectual property, disrupt operations, compromise products and services, and cause reputational or financial harm despite security controls and governance. A November 2022 incident at Jeppesen was found not to threaten flight safety and had no material impact, but future incidents could. Boeing also handles customer and supplier systems and data, whose compromise could cause losses. Physical or IT threats, extreme weather, climate impacts, natural disasters, and public-health crises could disrupt operations and suppliers, delay deliveries, reduce sales, raise costs, and damage Boeing’s reputation.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
key_items: The outcome of litigation and of government inquiries and investigations involving our business is unpredictable and an adverse decision in any such matter could have a material effect on our financial position and results of operations.
Our operations expose us to the risk of material environmental liabilities.; We may be adversely affected by global climate change or by legal, regulatory or market responses to such change.
Our operations expose us to the risk of material environmental liabilities.
We may be adversely affected by global climate change or by legal, regulatory or market responses to such change.
nodes.summary: Litigation and government inquiries or investigations are unpredictable, may divert resources, and could adversely affect financial results and cash flows. Environmental laws expose the company to cleanup costs, penalties, injury or property claims, and liabilities tied to its operations, acquired companies, or indemnities; stricter rules or newly discovered contamination could add costs. Climate change, ESG expectations, regulation, market and contractual demands, physical impacts, emissions standards, chemical restrictions, and water and waste requirements may raise costs, disrupt supply and production, limit products, and harm reputation or competitiveness. Failure to meet or accurately report sustainability goals could also damage reputation and access to capital.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity
key_items: We may be unable to obtain debt to fund our operations and contractual commitments at competitive rates, on commercially reasonable terms or in sufficient amounts.

Substantial pension and other postretirement benefit obligations have a material impact on our earnings, shareholders’ equity and cash flows from operations, and could have significant adverse impacts in future periods.
Our insurance coverage may be inadequate to cover all significant risk exposures.
A significant portion of our customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in certain types of Boeing aircraft, which exposes us to concentration risks.
nodes.summary: The text outlines financing and liquidity risks from substantial debt, upcoming repayments and aircraft financing commitments, potential credit downgrades, and constrained access to borrowing; pension and retiree health obligations affected by market and cost assumptions; potentially inadequate insurance or indemnification for liabilities, including aviation accidents; and customer, regional, and aircraft-type concentrations in the financing portfolio that could cause losses. It also warns that union or supplier work stoppages may disrupt production and revenue. Unresolved staff comments are not applicable.

nodes.title: Insurance, Financing, Labor, and Staff Comments Risks
key_items: Some of our and our suppliers’ workforces are represented by labor unions, which may lead to work stoppages.
nodes.summary: The page discusses potential liability and inadequate insurance for certain products, including risks from aircraft accident claims, and concentration risks in customer financing by customer, region, aircraft type, and credit quality. It describes how union representation, strikes, and supplier labor actions could disrupt production, strain customer relationships, and reduce revenue. Item 1B states that there are no unresolved staff comments.

nodes.title: Properties, Legal Proceedings, and Mine Safety
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2022, the company had about 87 million square feet of productive floor space, approximately 88% in the United States, distributed among its businesses and major locations worldwide. Runways and taxiways are generally shared airport facilities used under long-term government leases; the U.S. government also provides some facilities and equipment for contract work. The company is involved in legal proceedings, with related contingencies discussed in Note 21 of its consolidated financial statements. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: Boeing is a global aerospace leader serving commercial aviation, defense, space and related markets, with major U.S. operations and an expanding international network of partners and suppliers. Its strategy centers on Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, and Global Services, supported by Boeing Capital; earnings from these businesses fund new offerings. The company emphasizes market-driven products, efficiency, quality and shareholder returns. Its units focus respectively on leading commercial aviation, delivering cost-effective defense and space solutions while pursuing growth, providing comprehensive support services, and arranging selective customer financing.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: The text describes a recovering aviation market: domestic and regional travel and freighter demand are strengthening, while international and wide-body recovery remains constrained, particularly by COVID-related restrictions in China. Supply-chain disruption, labor instability, inflation, and factory inefficiencies are reducing productivity, harming financial results and cash flow. Airline losses and high costs create near-term risks, though long-term demand is positive, with projected 3.8% traffic growth and demand for about 41,170 new aircraft over 20 years; external shocks and environmental rules remain risks. BGS commercial services returned to pre-pandemic levels, with government-services demand stable. BDS demand is stable, but disruptions and fixed-price program charges threaten earnings and cash flow. The Ukraine war caused $212 million in first-quarter 2022 charges; Boeing closed Russian facilities, suspended Russia-related business, supports employee transfers, complies with sanctions, and monitors possible supply and customer impacts.

title: GAAP

nodes.title: Non-GAAP (1)
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents Boeing’s 2022–2020 GAAP and non-GAAP loss measures, margins, tax rates and per-share losses, noting that non-GAAP measures exclude certain pension and postretirement-benefit costs and directing readers to reconciliations. It lists annual revenues by business segment and total: revenue rose $4.322 billion in 2022, as higher Commercial Airplanes and Global Services revenue outweighed declines in Defense, Space & Security; it also rose $4.128 billion in 2021, driven by growth across the three segments. The excerpt explains the principal drivers, including aircraft deliveries, services volume, development-program charges and defense-program performance.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: The text presents Boeing’s 2020–2022 consolidated operating results and segment revenue and operating-loss tables, including GAAP and non-GAAP measures. In 2022, revenue rose 7% to $66.6 billion, while GAAP operating loss was $3.5 billion and core operating loss $4.7 billion. Revenue growth versus 2021 came mainly from higher 737 and 787 deliveries and commercial services, partly offset by lower Defense, Space & Security revenue due to development-program charges and weaker performance. The 2021 revenue increase reflected recovery in aircraft deliveries and services. Operating-loss trends and drivers include defense-program charges, the absence or presence of large 787 and 777X reach-forward losses, delivery and production changes, and services volume and mix. Core operating loss excludes FAS/CAS pension and postretirement service-cost adjustments; the text points to further reconciliations. Results remain exposed to supply-chain disruption, labor instability, and delivery ramp-up.

nodes.title: Loss From Operations
nodes.summary: The text reviews Boeing’s operating results and unallocated expenses for 2020–2022. It provides loss-from-operations and core operating-loss figures, explains year-over-year changes by segment—including development-program charges, deliveries, service volume, and prior-year reach-forward losses—and notes continuing supply-chain, labor, and delivery pressures. It details unallocated items such as share-based compensation, deferred compensation, R&D, and eliminations, including SEC settlement and DOJ-related charges. It also reports pension costs and FAS/CAS adjustments and refers readers to Note 16 for postretirement plans.

nodes.title: Other Earnings Items
nodes.summary: The table reports Boeing’s 2020–2022 operating losses, other income, interest and debt expense, pretax losses, income taxes, continuing-operation losses, noncontrolling interests, and net losses attributable to shareholders. Notes explain pension and postretirement income trends and their drivers, plus annual changes in interest expense. The text also summarizes the Inflation Reduction Act’s 15% corporate minimum tax and 1% stock-buyback excise tax, effective in 2023, which Boeing expects to have no material impact, and refers readers to Note 4 for tax details.

nodes.title: Total Costs and Expenses (“Cost of Sales”)
nodes.summary: Cost of sales includes materials, labor, overhead, and subcontracting; BCA generally uses program accounting, long-term contracts recognize costs as incurred, and spare parts use average cost. Cost of sales was $63.1 billion in 2022, up $3.8 billion year over year due mainly to BDS charges and higher BCA revenue; its share of revenue was largely unchanged. In 2021 it fell $4.6 billion from 2020, reflecting prior-year segment charges, partly offset by higher revenue and the 787 reach-forward loss; cost of sales as a revenue percentage also declined. R&D expense was $2.85 billion in 2022, up $603 million due to 777X, 737 MAX, and other product-development investment; it was $2.25 billion in 2021, down $227 million from 2020 due to lower BCA and enterprise investment and 777X spending.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: The table reports Boeing’s backlog at December 31, 2022 and 2021, by business segment and in contractual and unobligated categories. Total backlog rose from $377.5 billion to $404.4 billion. Contractual backlog excludes options, unsigned announced orders, terminable orders, and unauthorized government funding; it increased mainly from Commercial Airplanes, partly offset by Defense, Space & Security declines. Prolonged 737 MAX delivery constraints in China or further 777X and 737-7/-10 delays could reduce backlog or cause cancellations. Unobligated backlog increased mainly due to awards, partly offset by reclassifications.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: Boeing monitors global trade risks, including U.S.–China tariffs and stalled relations, steel and aluminum tariffs and agreements easing them with several trading partners, and Russia-related sanctions and export controls that could affect costs, supply chains, partners, or customers. Commercial Airplanes faces a recovering but highly competitive industry, with pandemic-related demand and production disruptions, dependence on global markets (about 70% of backlog is with non-U.S. airlines), and pressure from Airbus, COMAC, and other rivals benefiting in some cases from government support. The 737 MAX grounding weakened Boeing’s delivery share and may help competitors. Competition is intensifying in products, efficiency, pricing, and market share; Boeing is improving products and services, transforming its business, and addressing unfair competitor subsidies.

nodes.title: BCA Financial Results and Deliveries
nodes.summary: The page reports 2020–2022 revenues, share of company revenues, operating losses and margins, and R&D spending. BCA revenues rose in 2022 due mainly to higher 737 and 787 deliveries; the 2021 increase reflected 737 MAX’s return to service and the absence of 2020 customer-consideration charges, partly offset by fewer 787 deliveries. It also lists annual and cumulative 737, 747, 767, 777 and 787 deliveries, identifying intercompany deliveries in parentheses.

nodes.title: Loss From Operations
nodes.summary: BCA’s operating loss narrowed to $2.37 billion in 2022 from $6.475 billion in 2021, mainly due to higher 737 deliveries and lower abnormal production costs, partly offset by increased R&D, Ukraine-related charges and other expenses. 2022 abnormal costs totaled $1.753 billion across the 787, 777X and 737 programs. The 2021 loss included a $3.46 billion 787 reach-forward loss and production costs, partly offset by higher 737 MAX deliveries. The 2020 loss was $13.847 billion, driven by a $6.493 billion 777X reach-forward loss, pandemic-related delivery and margin declines, 737 costs and customer considerations, severance, frame repairs, and lower 787 margins; lower R&D partly offset these items.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: Defines backlog as probable, contingency-free consideration for unsatisfied or partly satisfied obligations, excluding conditional orders, options, BCC orders and terminable orders; it notes customer delivery remedies and ASC 606 adjustments. BCA backlog rose to $329.824 billion in 2022, despite $11.251 billion in cancellations and a $4.675 billion net ASC 606 reduction, and could fall with prolonged delivery or program delays. Explains accounting quantities, their role in margins, estimation inputs and quarterly review, then presents 2020–2022 program quantities, undelivered firm orders and cumulative firm orders for 737, 747, 767, 777/777X and 787 aircraft, including the military-derivative and BCC-order qualifications.

nodes.title: Program Highlights
nodes.summary: The text reviews Boeing Commercial Airplanes programs and development. For the 737, it covers rising accounting quantities and production, abnormal costs, global MAX return and China delivery uncertainty, inventory and remarketing, FAA certification and safety-retrofit requirements for the 737-7/-10, expected schedules, backlog, and risks. It notes 747 production ended, and describes 767 and 777/777X quantities, rates, margins, certification delays, production pause and costs, and potential losses. For the 787, it details resumed deliveries, inspections and rework, inventory, production plans, abnormal costs, and prior program loss. It also describes fleet-support services and costs, and development timelines subject to certification uncertainty.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: Commercial aircraft development and production require complex supplier coordination and skilled labor, and meeting customer, regulatory, performance, and reliability standards can be costly and technically difficult. New aircraft and derivatives face schedule and certification risks heightened by global scrutiny after the 737 MAX accidents. These factors threaten timely delivery and program profitability, including through changes in accounting quantities, product mix, costs, rates, escalation factors, reliability, capacity investment, learning, design changes, cost-reduction progress, regulatory requirements, testing, demand, and customer or supplier claims. Despite reasonable estimates, technical complexity may require additional costs or delay deliveries, potentially leading to terminations, cancellations, or other significant exposure.

nodes.title: United States Government Defense Environment Overview
nodes.summary: FY23 appropriations provided $817 billion for the DoD and $25.4 billion for NASA, funding Boeing programs including the F/A-18, F-15EX, Chinook, Apache, Osprey, KC-46A, MQ-25 and Space Launch System. Funding supports F/A-18 production into 2025 but excludes additional P-8 aircraft; P-8 seeks sales to extend production beyond 2024. FY24-and-beyond funding is uncertain, and spending pressures or budget changes could reduce, cancel or delay programs, materially affecting Boeing’s results, financial position or cash flows. Non-U.S. defense demand reflects evolving security threats and modernization needs; BDS sees opportunities in Asia, Europe and the Middle East, with non-U.S. customers representing 28% of its year-end 2022 backlog.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The text reports operating results for 2020–2022: revenue was $26,257 million, $26,540 million, and $23,162 million; operating earnings were $1,539 million, $1,544 million, and a $3,544 million loss, with margins of 5.9%, 5.8%, and -15.3%, respectively. It cautions that long, varied contract cycles and order structures make period results and backlog comparisons unreliable indicators of future performance. It also lists annual deliveries by aircraft, tanker, satellite, and other production categories, totaling 154 units in 2020, 169 in 2021, and 165 in 2022.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BDS revenue fell $3.378 billion in 2022 versus 2021, mainly due to development-program charges, other defense-program underperformance, and lower P-8 and weapons volume; cumulative contract catch-up adjustments were $1.858 billion more unfavorable, largely due to those charges. Revenue rose $283 million in 2021 versus 2020, primarily from higher KC-46A revenue after orders for 27 aircraft and lower charges, partly offset by declines in rotorcraft, Commercial Crew, and VC-25B. Catch-up adjustments were $56 million less unfavorable than in 2020.

nodes.title: (Loss)/earnings From Operations
nodes.summary: BDS reported a $3.544 billion operating loss in 2022, down $5.088 billion year over year, mainly from $4.284 billion in additional unfavorable contract catch-up adjustments, including charges on several fixed-price development programs; volume, mix and R&D also hurt results. 2021 earnings rose $5 million from 2020 as lower contract charges were offset by weaker rotorcraft volume and ULA equity earnings. Equity-method income was $13 million, $53 million and $141 million in 2022, 2021 and 2020. Backlog fell $5.455 billion to $54.373 billion, reflecting award and revenue timing. BDS discusses cost-type and fixed-price program risks, including technical, schedule and cost problems, reach-forward losses, and possible future charges or other material impacts. Global Services describes recovering commercial services demand, expected continued strength, long-term aftermarket growth and airline use of analytics and outsourced spares management; government-services demand remained stable in 2022, varying by fleet utilization and age, with the U.S. representing over half of markets served.

nodes.title: BDS Backlog and Development Program Risks
nodes.summary: BDS operating results include equity-method investment income, mainly from ULA and non-U.S. joint ventures; ULA earnings rose in 2022, partly offset by other investment losses. Year-end 2022 backlog was $54.373 billion, down $5.455 billion from 2021 due to award timing and revenue recognition. Development programs face technical, schedule, and cost risks: cost-type contracts may incur reduced fees, lower margins, or cancellation; fixed-price programs may incur reach-forward losses. Issues can increase costs, reduce prices, delay delivery, trigger termination or other significant exposure, and require future loss provisions. The text also introduces Global Services.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: BGS serves aerospace aftermarket, logistics, maintenance, training, and digital markets. Commercial services recovered to pre-pandemic levels in 2022, with long-term demand supported by fleet growth, efficiency and predictive-maintenance needs, and outsourced spare-parts management. Government demand was stable; U.S. growth is expected to be flat, while Middle East and Asia Pacific fleets grow faster. Aging military aircraft should sustain maintenance demand, though U.S. spending uncertainty may delay programs. Competition drives intense pricing pressure, and global market access is important. Revenues rose to $17.6 billion in 2022, mainly on commercial volume, and to $16.3 billion in 2021 on commercial and government volume. Operating earnings rose to $2.7 billion in 2022 on commercial volume and mix, and increased substantially in 2021 as 2020 pandemic-related charges eased; 2021 included a $220 million inventory write-down. The text details government-service declines, contract catch-up adjustments, and 2020 inventory, impairment, credit-loss, termination, facility, and severance charges.

nodes.title: BGS Market Outlook and Operating Results
nodes.summary: The text notes expected flat U.S. fleet growth, faster non-U.S. fleet additions, aging military aircraft driving service demand, U.S. government spending uncertainty, and intense aviation-services price competition. BGS revenues were $17.6 billion in 2022, $16.3 billion in 2021, and $15.5 billion in 2020; annual increases reflected higher services volume, partly offset by government-service declines and lower contract catch-up benefits. Operating earnings rose to $2.7 billion in 2022 and from $450 million in 2020 to $2.0 billion in 2021. Changes reflected commercial volume and mix, government performance, contract adjustments, COVID-related 2020 charges, and a 2021 inventory write-down.

nodes.title: Boeing Backlog and Capital Segment Results
nodes.summary: BGS backlog fell 6% in 2022, mainly from revenue recognized on earlier contracts. Boeing Capital’s $1.549 billion portfolio includes below-investment-grade customers and aircraft concentration; it provided $96 million in financing in 2022 and expects alternative funding sources. Parked aircraft declined to 18.3% of the western-built fleet, but potential retirements and further aircraft groundings pose risks to deliveries, customer payments, financing, and asset values. BCC results for 2020–2022 show 2022 revenue of $199 million and operating earnings of $29 million. Revenue decreased $73 million in 2022 due mainly to lower re-lease gains; operating earnings fell $77 million due to higher Ukraine-related loss allowances and lower revenue. 2021 earnings rose $43 million from 2020 on higher revenue and lower loss provisions, interest, and impairment expenses.

nodes.title: Financial Position
nodes.summary: BCC’s 2022 financial position shows a $226 million portfolio decline, mainly from run-off, and a 4.9-to-1 debt-to-equity ratio; intercompany guarantees and subsidies mitigate certain credit and impairment effects. Boeing’s cash-flow data and discussion cover 2020–2022: operating cash improved in 2022 due to working-capital changes, including liabilities, payables, inventory, customer advances, and tax refunds, partly offset by lower non-cash items and greater net loss; 2021–2020 comparisons cite the 787 loss, inventory trends, customer compensation, and other items. Supply-chain financing is immaterial. Investing cash flows reflect investment proceeds and capital spending, expected to rise in 2023. Financing flows reflect borrowing and repayments; debt balances and short-term portions are reported. Share repurchases remain suspended, employee tax-withholding shares were transferred, and dividends have been suspended since 2020.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The text summarizes Boeing’s year-end 2022 contractual cash obligations and liquidity, including cash, investments, credit facilities, debt ratings, market-access risks, and covenant compliance. It discusses pension funding status, contributions, and stock used for retirement plans; recorded and unrecorded purchase obligations, supplier commitments, and industrial participation agreements; off-balance-sheet guarantees; commercial commitments, especially aircraft financing; legal and environmental contingencies; and the purpose and limitations of non-GAAP core operating and earnings measures.

nodes.title: Commercial Commitments and Contingent Obligations
nodes.summary: The page notes purchase obligations through 2034, including industrial participation orders subject to supplier capability and competitiveness, and refers to off-balance-sheet arrangements and guarantees. It summarizes 2022 commercial commitments by type and timing: standby letters of credit and surety bonds, and aircraft financing commitments. Financing commitments rose to $16.1 billion from $12.9 billion in 2021; significant funding is not expected, though it cannot be ruled out, as third-party financing is pursued. Contingent obligations include legal proceedings, claims and investigations, and environmental remediation, for which a $752 million liability was recorded.

nodes.title: Core Operating Loss, Core Operating Margin and Core Loss Per Share
nodes.summary: The text explains that Boeing supplements GAAP results with non-GAAP core operating earnings, margin, and earnings per share, which should not replace or be viewed separately from GAAP measures and may differ across companies. Core measures exclude FAS/CAS service-cost adjustments; core EPS also excludes non-operating pension and postretirement costs. It describes how GAAP and CAS pension costs are calculated and allocated, reports related benefits for 2020–2022 and their causes, refers readers to further disclosures, and says management uses these measures to assess and forecast performance because excluded costs are largely market-driven or unallocable to government contracts.

nodes.title: Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures to GAAP Measures
nodes.summary: Reconciles 2020–2022 non-GAAP core operating loss, margins, and loss per share with comparable GAAP measures, with weighted-average diluted shares and notes explaining pension/postretirement service-cost adjustments, non-operating benefit expenses, and tax effects. Describes critical accounting policies for long-term contracts: performance obligations, revenue and cost estimates, key assumptions and risks, quarterly reviews, catch-up and reach-forward loss accounting, annual impacts and major 2022 program losses, and sensitivity to margin assumptions. Introduces program accounting’s requirement to reliably estimate revenues, costs, and margins across a defined production quantity.

nodes.title: Accounting for Long-term Contracts
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting estimates for long-term contracts at BDS and some BGS operations, generally treated as single performance obligations. Revenue and profit recognition depends on estimates of contract sales, costs, and margins, influenced by contract terms, government cost rules, inflation, technical and schedule risks, performance, labor, and other factors. Significant estimates are reviewed quarterly; revisions produce cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate reach-forward losses. These adjustments increased operating losses by $5.253 billion in 2022, $880 million in 2021, and $942 million in 2020, mainly due to losses on several fixed-price development programs, with future losses possible. Estimates may materially affect earnings; a one-percentage-point change in 2022 profitable-contract margins would alter pretax income by about $300 million. The text also introduces program accounting, which requires reliable estimates of revenue, costs, and gross margin across a defined production quantity.

nodes.title: Program Accounting
nodes.summary: The text explains Boeing’s critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and program accounting. Contract estimates of revenue, costs, and profit are reviewed quarterly; changes can trigger cumulative catch-up adjustments or immediate reach-forward losses. Loss adjustments increased operating losses by $5.253 billion in 2022, largely from several fixed-price development programs, with future losses possible; a 1% margin change could shift 2022 pretax income by about $300 million. Program accounting estimates quantities, prices, and costs, with quarterly reviews and losses recognized when costs exceed revenue. It highlights near-break-even 767, 777X, and 787 margins, 777X risks, and the 787’s 2021 $3.5 billion loss and 2022 quantity increase, while warning of possible further losses.

nodes.title: Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Most employees formerly covered by defined benefit plans have moved to a company-funded defined contribution plan. Annual pension measurements depend on assumptions such as discount rates and expected asset returns; changes or actual-versus-expected differences can affect expenses, obligations and shareholders’ equity. A 25-basis-point discount-rate increase or decrease changes the projected obligation by −$1,270 million or +$1,415 million, with no significant pension-cost impact. A 25-basis-point decrease or increase in expected returns would have raised or lowered 2022 pension cost by $158 million. Note 16 provides the assumptions for the past three years.

nodes.title: Deferred Income Taxes – Valuation Allowance
nodes.summary: At year-end 2022, the Company reported $12.301 billion in deferred tax assets, $9.306 billion in liabilities, and a $3.162 billion valuation allowance. It assesses realizability quarterly, weighing evidence; recent losses preclude projected earnings, so management uses judgment-based estimates of reversal timing. The allowance rose $739 million, mainly for unrealizable tax credits and carryforwards, partly offset by pension remeasurement; further increases may hurt earnings or other comprehensive income. Market-risk disclosures cover interest-rate exposure (not material), foreign-currency forwards (a 10% rate move changes unrealized losses by $232 million, offset by hedged items), and commodity hedges (a 10% price move changes unrealized losses by $70 million, likewise offset); combined exposures are not material.

nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The text notes potential tax valuation allowances and refers readers to the income tax financial-statement note. It then describes interest-rate risk from debt and customer financing: fixed-rate debt exposure is considered immaterial, there was no significant floating-rate debt at year-end 2022, and customer financing has historically had no material interest-rate effects. Foreign-currency forwards hedge committed and forecasted receipts and payments; a 10% exchange-rate move would change unrealized losses by $232 million, offset by remeasurement of hedged transactions, leaving no material combined market risk.

nodes.title: Commodity Price Risk
nodes.summary: The text describes commodity price risk from production-related purchases, mitigated using commodity swaps and purchase contracts. A 10% market-price change at December 31, 2022, would change unrealized derivative losses by $70 million, offset by gains or losses on hedged transactions; together, the contracts create no material market risk. It then provides the financial statements and supplementary data index, listing consolidated statements, business segment data, Notes 1–22 covering accounting policies and financial topics, and the independent auditor reports.

summary: Presents Boeing’s 2020–2022 GAAP and non-GAAP financial results, segment revenues, operating losses, margins, taxes, earnings per share, deliveries, and backlog, with reconciliations and explanations of key year-over-year drivers. Covers Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital performance, programs, markets, competition, government funding, and operational risks. Discusses costs, R&D, long-term contract and program accounting estimates, pension plans, deferred taxes, liquidity, cash flows, debt, capital resources, commitments, contingencies, and interest-rate, currency, and commodity risks, alongside relevant financial-statement notes and auditor reports.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Operations
key_items: Loss from operations; Loss before income taxes; Diluted loss per share
summary: The text presents Boeing’s consolidated statements of operations for 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions of dollars except per-share data. It lists product and service sales, total revenues, costs and expenses, investment results, administrative and research expenses, disposition gains, operating losses, other income and interest expense, pretax losses, income tax effects, net losses attributable to noncontrolling interests and Boeing shareholders, and basic and diluted loss per share. It refers readers to the financial statement notes on pages 59–114.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
summary: A table of contents entry presents Boeing’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income for 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions of dollars. It reports net loss; other comprehensive income or loss, net of tax, from currency translation, investments, derivative instruments, and defined-benefit pension and postretirement items; total other comprehensive income or loss; comprehensive income or loss; amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests; and comprehensive income or loss attributable to Boeing shareholders. Financial statement notes are referenced on pages 59–114.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Financial Position
summary: The text presents Boeing and subsidiaries’ consolidated statements of financial position at December 31, 2022 and 2021, in millions of dollars except per-share data. It lists assets, including current assets, customer financing, property and equipment, goodwill, intangibles, deferred taxes, investments, and other assets; liabilities, including current and long-term obligations, debt, and retiree and pension liabilities; and shareholders’ equity or deficit, noncontrolling interests, and total equity. Comparative balances are provided, with total assets and total liabilities and equity of $137,100 million in 2022 and $138,552 million in 2021. The statements refer readers to notes on pages 59–114.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows
summary: Boeing’s consolidated cash flow statement reports operating, investing, and financing cash flows for 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions of dollars. It details net losses and operating adjustments, including non-cash items and changes in assets and liabilities; capital spending, disposals, acquisitions, and investments; borrowing, debt repayment, stock-option activity, employee taxes, and dividends; and exchange-rate effects. It presents net cash flows, annual changes and opening and closing balances of cash including restricted cash, restricted cash included in investments, and ending cash equivalents, with a reference to the financial-statement notes.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Equity
summary: A Boeing consolidated statement of equity for 2020–2022, in millions of dollars except per-share data, reports beginning and year-end balances and changes in common stock, additional paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, and total equity. Changes include net losses, other comprehensive income or loss and related taxes, share-based compensation, treasury stock transactions for options, share-based plans, 401(k) contributions and pensions, and changes in noncontrolling interests. It refers readers to the financial statement notes on pages 59–114.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements Summary of Business Segment Data

nodes.title: Total revenues
nodes.summary: A table of contents for Boeing’s consolidated financial statement notes, listing a summary of business segment data in millions of dollars for years ended December 31. It covers revenues by Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, Boeing Capital, and unallocated items, eliminations and other, plus total revenues. It also lists operating earnings or losses by segment, segment operating loss, unallocated items, eliminations and other, and the FAS/CAS service cost adjustment.

nodes.title: Loss from operations
nodes.summary: The text presents Boeing’s 2020–2022 consolidated income statement results, including operating losses, other income, interest and debt expense, pretax losses, income taxes, net losses, and losses attributable to Boeing shareholders and noncontrolling interests. It then begins Note 1 on accounting policies: consolidation includes majority-owned subsidiaries and required variable-interest entities, eliminates intercompany transactions, and identifies four reportable segments. It explains estimation uncertainty, contract-based operating cycles, and revenue recognition and payment terms for commercial aircraft, including program accounting, plus the products and services covered by long-term government and other customer contracts.

nodes.title: Boeing Accounting Policies and Financial Statement Basis
key_items: Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies Principles of Consolidation and Basis of Presentation
nodes.summary: Boeing’s consolidated financial statements cover the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020, and include majority-owned subsidiaries and required variable interest entities; significant intercompany accounts and transactions are eliminated. Boeing reports four segments: Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital. Preparing statements under U.S. GAAP requires estimates and assumptions, so actual results may differ. For some current asset and liability classifications, Boeing uses the related contract or program duration as its operating cycle, generally longer than one year.

nodes.title: Revenue and Related Cost Recognition
nodes.summary: Describes revenue and cost accounting for commercial aircraft, long-term contracts, spare parts, other services, concessions, contract assets/liabilities, financial services, and reinsurance. It explains transaction-price allocation, point-in-time versus over-time recognition, progress measurement, variable consideration, payment terms, financing and collectability, lease income and asset valuation, and estimates for contract costs, catch-up adjustments, and losses—including major program losses and reported impacts. It also outlines research and development expense, customer-funded arrangements, and bid-and-proposal costs.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies for customer financing receivables, including when income recognition is suspended, how past-due and non-accrual status are determined, and how lease or interest income is recognized for non-accrual customers. It covers residual-value estimates and impairment, operating-lease revenue, depreciation, held-for-sale assets and impairment testing. It reports Astro Ltd.’s workers’ compensation reinsurance revenues and costs for 2020–2022, presented net in cost of sales. It also explains research and development expense recognition, treatment of customer-funded arrangements and bid-and-proposal costs, with annual amounts for 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Compensation, Taxes, and Retirement Benefits
nodes.summary: Describes share-based compensation measurement for share- and cash-settled awards and expense recognition over vesting. Explains income tax provisions, uncertain tax positions, related interest and penalties, and valuation allowances for deferred tax assets. Summarizes pension and other retiree health benefits, plan transitions and benefit factors, actuarial cost assumptions and gain/loss treatment, and reporting of funded status.

nodes.title: Postemployment, Environmental, and Cash Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Postemployment benefit liabilities are recorded when payment is probable, estimable, and tied to vested or accumulated rights. Environmental remediation exposures are assessed using studies, expert analyses, and legal reviews; probable, estimable costs are accrued at the best estimate or low end of a reasonable range, without discounting, and recoveries are recognized when probable. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less. Bank balances are aggregated when set-off rights apply; negative balances, mainly uncleared checks, are reclassified to accounts payable and totaled $102 and $47 at year-end 2022 and 2021, respectively.

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.summary: Inventories include direct engineering, production, tooling, other nonrecurring costs, and applicable overhead, capped at net realizable value; abnormal or inappropriately allocated fixed costs are expensed. Some long-cycle costs extend beyond one year, and federal contract inventory includes allowable manufacturing-reengineering costs. Commercial program inventory includes deferred early-unit production costs, expected to be recovered over the accounting quantity, and supplier advances amortized as parts arrive. Quarterly reviews assess contract and program completion costs and revenues; expected losses are provisioned. Used aircraft and general materials are carried at cost up to net realizable value, while spare parts use the lower of average cost or net realizable value; impaired, excess, or obsolete stock is expensed. Airline early issue sales consideration is recorded in inventory and reduces revenue upon aircraft delivery; unrecoverable amounts are written off if customers fail to take delivery.

nodes.title: Precontract Costs
nodes.summary: Precontract costs expected to be recovered from future orders are capitalized in inventory, except start-up costs, which are expensed; capitalized costs are written off if recovery becomes unlikely. Property and equipment are recorded at cost, including construction-period interest, and depreciated using specified lives and methods; internal-use software and software-as-a-service costs are capitalized in other assets and amortized over five years or the hosting term. Useful lives are periodically reviewed; assets held for sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value less selling costs, while held-for-use assets are assessed for impairment and written down when unrecoverable. Lease classification is assessed at inception; operating lease assets and liabilities are recorded in other assets and accrued or long-term liabilities, while finance-lease assets, primarily computer equipment, are included in property and equipment.

nodes.title: Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for commercial aircraft program losses, inventory valuation and impairment, and airline early issue sales consideration, including potential write-offs. It describes capitalization and recovery testing of precontract costs. Property and equipment policies cover cost, useful lives, depreciation methods, software amortization, held-for-sale measurement, and impairment. Lease policies address classification and balance-sheet presentation, operating lease measurement using present-value payments and incremental borrowing rates, variable costs, term options, straight-line expense, and combining real-property lease and non-lease components.

nodes.title: Asset Retirement Obligations
nodes.summary: The company records known asset retirement obligations when fair value is reasonably estimable, including certain asbestos removal, decommissioning, and lease restoration obligations; recorded amounts are immaterial. Known conditional obligations are not recorded when timing or settlement methods are insufficiently known, but will be recognized once estimable. Potential obligations not yet discovered, such as unknown asbestos, are also excluded from the financial statements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for goodwill and acquired intangibles: impairment testing for indefinite-lived assets, IPR&D capitalization and reclassification, and finite-lived asset amortization periods and impairment. It describes accounting and impairment reviews for time deposits, available-for-sale debt securities, equity-method and other equity investments, plus classification of investment gains and losses as operating or non-operating. It also covers derivative fair-value recognition, cash-flow hedge accounting, and immediate earnings recognition for derivatives not designated as hedges, including aluminum purchase and sale agreements.

nodes.title: Investment and Derivative Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Finite-lived acquired intangibles are amortized over estimated useful lives and tested for impairment when indicators arise, with losses based on carrying value versus fair value. Time deposits are carried at cost; available-for-sale debt securities are fair-valued, with unrealized gains or losses in other comprehensive income, specific-identification realized gains or losses, and quarterly impairment reviews. Equity investments use the equity method, fair value, or adjusted cost depending on influence and valuation availability; applicable investments are tested quarterly. Investment income is classified as operating or non-operating. Derivatives are fair-valued; cash flow hedge gains and losses move from comprehensive income to earnings when the hedged transaction affects earnings, while non-designated aluminum and other derivatives’ fair-value changes enter earnings immediately.

nodes.title: Financial Asset Loss Allowances and Aircraft Trade-ins
key_items: Allowances for Losses on Certain Financial Assets
nodes.summary: The page explains quarterly assessment of credit-loss allowances using customer creditworthiness, receivable characteristics, expected losses, and collateral values; aircraft collateral is valued using third-party publications and, when needed, specific judgment. Some agreements allow other customer assets to cover collateral shortfalls. It also describes aircraft trade-in commitments, including revenue adjustments for price-versus-fair-value differences and charges for subsequent value declines, with estimates accrued as liabilities. Trade-in values reflect aircraft attributes, market conditions, likely resale, leasing, or scrap markets, and quarterly valuation updates.

nodes.title: Warranties, Supplier Penalties, and Guarantees
nodes.summary: Describes BCA and BDS product warranties, their coverage and terms, how standard and exceptional warranty costs and liabilities are estimated and recorded, and how aircraft performance guarantees and supplier claims are accounted for. Supplier penalties are accrued when probable and reasonably estimable. Guarantees are initially recorded at fair value; credit-guarantee expected losses reflect default risk and recoveries, with contingent-loss liabilities adjusted quarterly.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: Note 2 reports goodwill by business segment for 2020–2022, including adjustments that reduced total goodwill from $8.081 billion to $8.057 billion. It gives carrying amounts of indefinite-lived trade names ($197 million) and in-process research and development ($202 million) for 2021 and 2022, and gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization of finite-lived acquired intangibles by category for both years. It also notes $178 million of 2020 distribution-rights impairments, amortization expense of $241 million in 2022 and $284 million in 2021, and estimated annual amortization of $234 million, $219 million, $194 million, $190 million, and $172 million for 2023–2027.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: The note explains that basic and diluted EPS use the two-class method, allocating undistributed earnings equally between common shares and participating securities. It defines both calculations and reports 2022–2020 net losses, weighted-average share counts, and basic and diluted loss per share. It identifies dilutive instruments and deferred-compensation participating securities. Potential shares were excluded as antidilutive during the loss periods; a table lists excluded performance awards, performance-based and standard restricted stock units, and stock options that may dilute EPS in future periods.

nodes.title: Note 4 – Income Taxes
nodes.summary: Note 4 reports 2020–2022 pretax losses, current and deferred income taxes, cash tax refunds/payments, and reconciles statutory to actual tax, including CARES Act NOL carrybacks and a 2020 audit settlement. It details deferred tax assets/liabilities by category, NOL and credit expiration periods, and explains valuation allowances, loss history, reversal timing, and 2022 allowance changes. It also addresses indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings, insignificant tax interest and penalties, unrecognized tax benefits, and federal, state, and international audit years and status.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Accounts Receivable, net
nodes.summary: Note 5 reports accounts receivable, net, at December 31 for 2021 and 2022. Categories are U.S. government contracts, Commercial Airplanes, Global Services, Defense, Space, & Security, and Other, with a valuation allowance deducted; totals are $2,517 million for 2021 and $2,641 million for 2022. U.S. government contracts include foreign military sales through the U.S. government; the other listed business categories exclude U.S. government contracts.

nodes.title: Financial Asset Loss Allowances and Inventories
key_items: Note 6 – Allowances for Losses on Financial Assets
nodes.summary: Note 6 presents the 2021–2022 rollforward of expected credit loss allowances across accounts receivable, unbilled receivables, other current assets, customer financing, and other assets, including estimates, write-offs, and recoveries. Note 7 reports inventory categories and totals for 2022 and 2021, including contracts in progress, aircraft programs, capitalized precontract costs, and spare parts and other materials. A footnote identifies 2022 precontract costs related to KC-46A Tanker, Commercial Crew, and T-7 Production Options and refers to Note 13.

nodes.title: Commercial Aircraft Programs
nodes.summary: Commercial aircraft program inventory declined in 2022 as lower 737 and 787 inventory outweighed 777X growth; it included about 250 737s and 100 787s, versus 335 and 110 in 2021. The text details 737 deferred production and tooling costs and expected recovery from firm and future orders. 777X work in process, deferred production, and tooling costs rose; a 2022–23 production pause caused $325 in abnormal costs, and margins were near break-even. The 787 had a $3.46 billion 2021 reach-forward loss, specified deferred production, supplier advance, and tooling balances, expected recovery from firm and future orders, and abnormal costs of $1.24 billion in 2022 and $468 million in 2021 due to low production rates. Early issue sales consideration to airline customers was $3.586 billion in 2022, versus $3.290 billion in 2021.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: Unbilled receivables rose from $8.620 billion in 2021 to $8.634 billion in 2022, mainly due to BGS revenue exceeding billings, partly offset by BDS billings exceeding revenue. Advances and progress billings increased from $52.980 billion to $53.081 billion, mainly from BCA order advances, partly offset by BDS and BGS revenue recognition. Revenue recognized from beginning-of-year advances was $12.087 billion in 2022 and $11.336 billion in 2021. The table reports 2022 and 2021 unbilled contract assets and claims, including current and after-one-year amounts and valuation allowances. Commercial-incentive receivables expected after one year were $117 million and $131 million, respectively. Claim-related unbilled receivables are considered earned but subject to uncertainty in determination or realization.

nodes.title: Note 9 – Customer Financing
nodes.summary: Note 9 describes customer financing, mainly in the BCC segment, including leases generally lasting 1–12 years that may be extended, terminated, or allow aircraft purchase at a specified price. At year-end 2022 versus 2021, net financing receivables were $1.134 billion versus $1.338 billion, operating lease equipment was $470 million versus $474 million, and total customer financing was $1.604 billion versus $1.812 billion. The note details lease investment components, including payments, residual values, and unearned income; $405 million and $378 million of receivables were on non-accrual status, and the 2022 allowance increase was mainly due to the Ukraine war. Financing interest income was $13 million and $18 million, respectively, with no past-due receivables in 2022. It also presents 2022 receivables by credit rating and origination year, and reports allowance default rates of 100.0% for CCC, 31.5% for B, 2.9% for BB, and 0.1% for BBB.

nodes.title: Customer Financing Exposure
nodes.summary: Customer financing exposure is concentrated in 717, 747-8, 737, 777, MD-80, 757, and 747-400 aircraft, with balances shown for 2021 and 2022 and some amounts classified as operating or sales-type/finance leases. Operating lease equipment mainly comprises large commercial jets. Impairment charges for customer financing operating lease assets are reported for 2020–2022, including Boeing Capital and other Boeing amounts. Lease income in 2021–2022 and commencement profit on sales-type leases are disclosed. Expected undiscounted receipts over the next five years and thereafter are presented for notes receivable and both lease types, with imputed interest and unguaranteed residual values; unguaranteed residuals were $86 million in 2022 versus $110 million in 2021, and guaranteed residuals were not significant in 2022.

nodes.title: Note 10 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 10 reports property, plant and equipment balances at December 31, 2022 and 2021, including land, buildings and improvements, machinery and equipment, construction in progress, gross assets, accumulated depreciation and net totals. It gives depreciation expense for 2022–2020 and capitalized interest for those years, plus non-cash property acquisitions and accounts payable for property purchases in 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Investments and Equity Method Holdings
nodes.summary: Note 11 reports investment balances at December 31, 2022 and 2021, including equity method investments, time deposits, available-for-sale debt, equity and other investments, and restricted cash. It notes dividends received, undistributed equity-method earnings, the 2021 HorizonX deconsolidation and related gain, and the purposes of restricted funds. Available-for-sale instruments are investment grade, with no credit-loss allowance recognized in 2022. The page also details equity-method investment balances by investment, segment, and ownership percentage.

nodes.title: Note 12 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 12 reports operating leases for facilities, warehouses, and offices: 2022 and 2021 expenses, variable costs, cash payments, and new-lease noncash additions; year-end right-of-use assets, current and noncurrent liabilities, remaining terms and discount rates; five-year and later payment maturities, imputed interest, and $420 million of leases commencing in 2023 for 3–25 years, primarily an aircraft-support hangar. Note 13 lists accrued liabilities for 2022 and 2021, including compensation, 737 MAX and other customer concessions, environmental costs, warranties, forward losses, interest, lease and retiree obligations, and other items.

nodes.title: 737 MAX Grounding
nodes.summary: The table reports the 737 MAX customer concessions and other considerations liability declining from $5.537 billion at the start of 2021 to $2.940 billion at year-end 2021, then to $1.864 billion at year-end 2022, reflecting payments, in-kind concessions, and estimate changes. The 2022 balance includes $1.6 billion contracted and $0.3 billion under negotiation. Contracted amounts comprise $0.8 billion in reduced delivery payments, $0.7 billion cash, and $0.1 billion other concessions; cash payments include $0.1 billion in 2023 and $0.6 billion in later years. The form of the negotiated concessions depends on customer discussions.

nodes.title: Environmental
nodes.summary: Environmental remediation liabilities rose from $605 million in 2021 to $752 million in 2022, reflecting payments and estimate changes. Recorded amounts represent the best estimate or low end of reasonably possible costs, including up to 30 years of site operations and maintenance; costs may exceed reserves, and some obligations cannot be estimated. The high-end estimate exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,058 million in 2022 and $1,094 million in 2021. Product warranty liabilities increased from $1,900 million to $2,275 million, based on current-year additions, payments, and estimate changes. Aircraft trade-in commitments let certain customers exchange used aircraft at agreed prices; exercise likelihood is assessed periodically, and agreements have specified windows and notice requirements. Further losses remain possible. At year-end, it had about $180 in capitalized precontract costs and $159 in potential supplier termination liabilities for unauthorized future missions.

nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Boeing’s 2020–2022 financial statements fairly present its financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and separately reports an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, auditor independence, and PCAOB audit procedures designed to provide reasonable assurance against material misstatement. nodes.title: Cost Estimates for Fixed-Price Development Contracts — Refer to Notes 1 and 13 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns cost-to-complete estimates and margins on fixed-price development contracts, where revenue is recognized over time using costs incurred to measure progress. Complex contracts, limited historical data, uncertain costs, and supply-chain disruption, labor shortages, and inflation heighten the risk of lower margins or reach-forward losses and require significant judgment and specialized audit effort. For the KC-46A, Commercial Crew, VC-25B, T-7A, and MQ-25 contracts, auditors assessed estimation methods, assumptions, ranges and estimate changes; interviewed project personnel; observed work sites; tested data and compared independent expectations with management’s estimates; reviewed past estimates against actual results; and tested related internal controls.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Estimates for the 777X Program — Refer to Notes 1, 7, and 22 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns uncertainty in Boeing’s 777X program accounting estimates for customer demand, revenue, costs, certification effort and timing, and potential margin reductions or reach-forward losses. Auditing these estimates required extensive effort, judgment, and specialized expertise. Procedures included assessing sales campaigns and market demand against external sources; comparing revenue estimates with historical outcomes; evaluating methods and assumptions for revenue and costs; discussing certification challenges and timelines with responsible personnel; reviewing regulatory communications for contradictory evidence; and testing controls over judgments, assumptions, data, and calculations.

nodes.title: Program Accounting Revenue Estimates for the 787 Program — Refer to Notes 1, 7, and 22 to the financial statements
key_items: How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The text describes a critical audit matter concerning Boeing’s 787 program revenue estimates: production-quality and supply-chain problems make delivery schedules and customer compensation for delays uncertain, potentially reducing margins or causing reach-forward losses. Deloitte assessed management assumptions, methods, customer contracts, estimates, and related controls. Deloitte also reported an unqualified opinion that Boeing maintained effective internal control over financial reporting at December 31, 2022, and explained the audit basis and the purpose and limitations of such controls. The report is dated January 27, 2023; Deloitte has served as auditor since at least 1934.

Management is responsible for maintaining and assessing controls; the auditor explains its PCAOB registration, independence, audit responsibilities, reasonable-assurance objective, risk assessment, control testing, and basis for its opinion.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Internal control over financial reporting is designed to provide reasonable assurance that external financial statements comply with GAAP. It includes policies and procedures for accurate records of transactions and assets; authorized recording of transactions, receipts, and expenditures; and preventing or timely detecting unauthorized asset use or disposition that could materially affect financial statements. Such controls cannot guarantee prevention or detection of misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline as conditions change or compliance deteriorates. Deloitte & Touche LLP signed the statement in Chicago on January 27, 2023.

title: ARTICLE I Introduction
summary: The Boeing Company Executive Supplemental Savings Plan has four components: elective salary and incentive deferrals; restoration of 401(k) benefits limited by tax-code caps; executive benefits, including specified company contributions; and accounts transferred from a frozen deferred compensation plan.
